For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”<sup>28</sup>Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.<sup>29</sup>But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.<sup>30</sup>But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.”<sup>31</sup>So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.

5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the hinge on which the entire letter turns from theology to life. The freedom Paul has argued for throughout — freedom from the law as a system of justification, freedom from the curse, freedom from the elementary principles of the old age — must now be shown to produce not moral chaos but something far better than law-keeping ever could. The chapter answers two questions that the letter’s argument raises: What does this freedom look like in practice? And what is its alternative to the law as the shaping force of Christian behavior?

The answer to the first question is given negatively and positively. Negatively: freedom is not license (“do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh”). The Judaizers’ accusation — that a gospel without law-requirements would produce moral anarchy — is not left unanswered. But the answer is not to reinstate the law; the answer is to walk in the Spirit. Positively: the whole law is fulfilled in one word — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (v. 14). Those who walk by the Spirit do not need the law to produce love, because the Spirit is the Spirit of the God who is love, and his fruit in the believer is love. The Judaizers’ program produced biting and devouring; the Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

The heart of the chapter is the contrast between the works of the flesh (vv. 19–21) and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 22–23). The language itself is instructive: works (plural, produced by human striving) versus fruit (singular, the organic product of the Spirit’s life within). The flesh produces a catalogue of self-serving, community-destroying behaviors; the Spirit produces a coherent, integrated character that is nothing less than the character of Christ. The goal of the Christian life is not the avoidance of the flesh’s works by rule-keeping but the cultivation of the Spirit’s life by staying close to the one who gives it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 compresses four chapters into a line: for freedom Christ has set us free. The apparent tautology is the point — freedom is the destination, not a stage on the way to a stricter religion. Stand firm is a military verb, because freedom is not a resting state; slavery is restful in a way liberty is not, since a slave always knows where he stands. The yoke of slavery is Peter’s own phrase for the law at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:10), and it sits against the yoke Jesus offers in Matthew 11:29–30. Nobody goes without a yoke; the question is whose.

Verses 2–3 are the warning. If a man accepts circumcision as what completes his standing, Christ is of no advantage to him — not less, none, because he has changed systems into one that has no column for what somebody else has done. Verse 3 closes the escape route: he is obligated to keep the whole law, not the one item he was sold. Verse 4 states the result in two phrases that describe a change of position rather than of behaviour: severed from Christ, fallen out of the sphere of grace. Verse 5 draws the line with an emphatic we ourselves, and adds the note of waiting; v. 6 says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts, but faith working through love.

Then the appeal. Verse 7 uses a technical word for cutting in on a runner — somebody stepped into their lane. Verse 8 says quietly that this persuasion is not from him who calls them. Verse 9 warns that a little leaven changes the whole loaf, invisibly, while it is happening. Verse 10 is the surprise: Paul is confident about them, in the Lord, and leaves the troubler to God. Verse 11 shows what was being said about him and names the offence of the cross, and v. 12 aims a deliberately shocking wish at teachers who make the knife the mechanism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

The Reformed tradition has always held that gospel freedom is more than freedom from sin’s penalty; it is freedom from performance-based religion — liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. This is not antinomianism. The law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk in the Spirit rather than imposed from without on those who must earn a standing. Luther’s paradox holds both: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.

Verse 4 must be read for what it says. Both its clauses describe position, not conduct: the people addressed have become more religious, not less, and Paul identifies them in the same breath as those who would be justified by the law. To fall from grace here is to step off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, where Christ’s work is inoperative — not to have disgraced oneself, which is the phrase’s modern and quite different meaning. That Paul writes v. 10 six sentences later, expressing confidence about the very same people, settles how v. 4 is functioning: it is the warning that prevents the thing it describes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade — a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it is not an upgrade but an exchange, and v. 3 reads them the rest of the contract nobody mentioned. Verse 11 reveals that Paul was being quoted against himself, perhaps on the strength of his past; his answer is his scars. Verse 12 would have landed with local force, since the mother goddess, whose chief shrine was at Pessinus, was served by priests who castrated themselves.

Now:Standing firm (v. 1) usually means refusing to answer “where do I stand with God today?” by reaching for the last few days. Verse 4 describes a man at peace with being justified by his own record, which is the opposite of the reader it frightens; and v. 8 gives a usable test for any new teaching — does it come to you the way the God who called you came to you?

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ freed us so that we would live free; to submit again to the law as a way of acceptance is to put the yoke back on.

For freedom. Freedom is the purpose of our redemption, not a by-product.

Stand firm. Freedom must be defended.

A yoke of slavery. Peter called the law a yoke no one could bear (Acts 15:10). Christ’s yoke is easy (Matthew 11:30).

On a Tuesday. Freedom in Christ is not freedom to sin, but freedom from earning God’s love. Enjoy it.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals — a picture of burdensome obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accepting circumcision as necessary for salvation means losing Christ, and obligating oneself to keep the whole law.

No advantage. Christ plus anything equals no Christ.

The whole law. Circumcision was the entrance to the whole system of law-keeping.

What it does not mean. Circumcision itself is morally neutral (v. 6); the problem is trusting it.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who seek to be justified by the law have cut themselves off from Christ and from the way of grace.

Severed. Cut off, estranged.

Fallen away from grace. Where Christians differ. Arminians read this as true believers losing salvation. Reformed interpreters read it as abandoning the principle of grace for the principle of law: you cannot hold both. Verdict: “falling from grace” here means turning from grace to law as the way of justification, not falling into sin; Paul hopes and expects that they will not finally do so (v. 10).

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith and through the Spirit, believers wait for the final verdict of righteousness, and what matters is faith working through love.

The hope of righteousness. The final declaration at the judgment, already pronounced in justification.

Faith working through love. Where Christians differ. Roman Catholic theology read this as “faith formed by love” justifying. The Reformers answered that faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone: it works through love. Verdict: love is the fruit of justifying faith, not its ground.

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were running the race well until someone tripped them; this persuasion did not come from God, and a little leaven spreads.

Who hindered you? Like a runner cut in on.

A little leaven. Small errors spread (1 Corinthians 5:6).
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is confident in the Lord about the Galatians, and the troublemakers will bear God’s judgment.

Still preaching circumcision? If Paul preached the law, the offence of the cross would vanish. The cross offends because it leaves us nothing to contribute.

Emasculate themselves. A savage piece of sarcasm: if they are so keen on cutting, let them go the whole way, like the castrated priests of Cybele in Galatia.

On a Tuesday. The cross still offends. Do not soften it to make it acceptable.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele in that region, who castrated themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They were called to freedom, but they must not use it as an excuse for the flesh; instead they should serve one another in love. The whole law is summed up in one command, to love your neighbour as yourself. If they bite and devour one another, they will be destroyed by each other.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

The relation of law and love in Reformed ethics is exact. The law’s moral demands are not abolished for the believer; they are fulfilled, but from a different source and in a different direction. The law compels from outside and leaves the sinner exposed; love, produced by the Spirit, constrains from within and overflows. This is what the older divines meant by the law written on the heart (Jer. 31:33) — not a different law, but the same law internalised by the Spirit of adoption and obeyed as the expression of a heart that loves the God who gave everything, rather than as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also settles the charge of antinomianism that has followed the doctrine of free grace since the first century. Paul concedes the danger frankly and then refuses the remedy his opponents wanted. That refusal is the test of whether a man has understood the gospel he preaches: it is easy to answer licence with law, and it undoes everything. And v. 15 exposes the mechanism by which a doctrine of performance destroys a congregation — once standing is earned, every other believer becomes a measurement, and the resulting suspicion has a righteous vocabulary to conduct itself in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy, which is not an irony but a mechanism. The very community the Judaizers claimed to be perfecting by law-observance was tearing itself apart, and vv. 13–14 name the only thing that binds a church in the way rules never can.

Now:A church that makes the Christian life primarily about observable markers will always produce the same social weather: pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, comparison, and division. The cure v. 13 offers is not a new rule but service, given concretely to the person you are still disagreeing with.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Freedom is not licence for the flesh but freedom to serve one another in love, which fulfils the law.

An opportunity. A military word: a base of operations.

Serve. Douleuete, be slaves to one another. Freed from the law’s yoke, we take the yoke of love.

One word. Love your neighbour as yourself (Leviticus 19:18; Romans 13:8–10).

parallels.desc: you shall love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A church that bites and devours itself will be consumed.

Bite and devour. Like wild animals: slander, sarcasm and campaigns against one another.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must never disagree or correct; Paul does both in this letter. The sin is attacking people to wound rather than to restore.

On a Tuesday. Online and in church meetings, refuse the bite.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to walk by the Spirit, and they will not carry out the desires of the flesh, for the two are opposed and at war within them. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law. The works of the flesh are plain: sexual sin, impurity, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousy, rage, rivalry, divisions, envy, drunkenness and the like, and those who live this way will not inherit God’s kingdom. The Spirit produces a very different harvest: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, against which no law stands. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions. Since they live by the Spirit, they should keep in step with him, and not become conceited, provoking or envying one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification and Vivification, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

Reformed theology has always described the Christian life as two complementary movements: mortification, the putting to death of the flesh, which v. 24 states as something already done to every believer; and vivification, the coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The mortification is the application to daily life of what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the vivification is the fruit of the Spirit’s indwelling. The believer does not produce either. He participates in both by faith.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image itself. Crucifixion was chosen by Rome precisely because it was slow: a man nailed to a beam was mortally wounded, fixed, going nowhere — and still perfectly capable of shouting. That is the flesh in a believer. Its authority is broken and its outcome settled, and it will go on being audible until the body dies. Verse 21 must be read with the same care. Scripture never confuses a man who falls into a ditch with a man who lives in it, and the ache that makes a tender conscience afraid of that verse is itself the evidence the verse is not describing him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third. Verse 20 would have been the most uncomfortable line in the letter read aloud in those congregations, since the middle of Paul’s list of fleshly works is a description of what was happening in the room. Verse 25 carries a piece of quiet artistry: stoichōmen, keep in step, is built on the same root as the stoicheia that had them in bondage in 4:3 and 4:9. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

Now:Walking by the Spirit (v. 16) is concrete rather than mystical: asking before the difficult conversation rather than after it, going where he speaks often enough to know his voice, and obeying the small prompt you would rather not have noticed. And v. 26 has a test anyone can run: what happens in you when good news is announced about the believer whose life is flourishing most visibly?

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking by the Spirit is the way to resist the flesh, for Spirit and flesh are at war in every believer.

Walk by the Spirit. Daily dependence and obedience.

The flesh. Our sinful nature, still present.

Opposed. The Christian life is a battle.

Where Christians differ: sanctification. Some (perfectionists and some holiness teachers) promise an experience that ends the struggle. Reformed theology holds that the conflict continues until death, though the Spirit gives real victory (Romans 7:14–25; 8:13). Verdict: progressive sanctification: real growth, ongoing struggle, final perfection in glory.

Not under the law. Led by the Spirit, not driven by rules.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The works of the flesh are obvious, and those who live by them will not inherit God’s kingdom.

The list. Sexual sins, religious sins (idolatry, sorcery), social sins (enmity, strife, jealousy, rage, rivalry, division, envy) and sins of excess (drunkenness, orgies). Most are sins of relationship.

Sorcery. Pharmakeia: magic, often involving drugs.

The words. Sexual immorality: any sex outside marriage. Impurity: moral uncleanness in thought and act. Sensuality: shameless indulgence. Idolatry: giving to anything the place of God. Enmity: settled hostility. Strife: quarrelling. Jealousy: resenting another’s good. Fits of anger: outbursts of rage. Rivalries: selfish ambition, putting yourself forward. Dissensions and divisions: splitting into factions. Envy: wanting what another has, and wishing they had not. Drunkenness and orgies: drinking and partying without restraint.

Will not inherit. A settled practice of these marks someone outside the kingdom (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

What it does not mean. Not that one lapse shuts a believer out, nor that anger or desire are always sinful. Paul describes a life that does these things as its way of being.
verseByVerse.note: “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit produces in believers the character of Christ: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

The words. Love: self-giving care for others’ good (1 Corinthians 13). Joy: gladness in God that does not depend on circumstances. Peace: settled rest with God and harmony with others. Patience: long-suffering, slow to anger with people. Kindness: generous goodwill in action. Goodness: moral excellence that does good, even when that means correcting. Faithfulness: reliability, keeping your word. Gentleness: strength under control, meekness. Self-control: mastery of desires, the opposite of the drunkenness and orgies just named.

Fruit, singular. One harvest with nine qualities, growing together.

Not works but fruit. The flesh works; the Spirit grows.

Against such things there is no law. No law can produce them, and none forbids them.

What it does not mean. Not that believers produce these by trying harder, nor that effort has no place. Fruit grows where the tree is planted: we stay near Christ through his word, prayer and his people, and fight sin (v. 24), and the Spirit grows the fruit.

On a Tuesday. Which of the nine is weakest in you? Pray for the Spirit to grow it, and look for chances to practise it today.

For worship. Each fruit is a portrait of Jesus. Praise him.
verseByVerse.note: “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who belong to Christ have decisively crucified the flesh with its desires.

Passions and desires. Sinful longings, not every desire: hunger and love for a spouse are not crucified but ordered.

Have crucified. A completed act at conversion (Romans 6:6), worked out daily (Luke 9:23).

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since the Spirit gives us life, we must keep in step with him.

Keep in step. A military word: march in line behind a leader.
verseByVerse.note: “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spirit-led people do not compete for honour, provoke or envy one another.

Conceited. Empty glory.

On a Tuesday. Envy and competition creep into ministry too. Rejoice when others are honoured.

6.title: Boasting Only in the Cross: The New Creation and the Community of Grace
6.overview:
The letter’s final chapter moves from the Spirit’s inner work to its outward expression in the community of faith. The freedom of the gospel, Paul has shown, is not moral permissiveness; it is the freedom that produces love, and love expresses itself in the concrete practices of the community. Chapter 6 describes what the community shaped by the gospel looks like: it bears burdens, restores the fallen gently, gives generously, sows to the Spirit, and refuses to grow weary in doing good.

The chapter reaches its climax in Paul’s autographic conclusion (vv. 11–18), where he returns one final time to the contrast that has driven the entire letter. The Judaizers boast in their circumcision program; they want to make a good showing in the flesh, to avoid persecution for the cross. Paul boasts in nothing except the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ — the event that crucified the world to him and him to the world. And this cross has created something radically new: not merely reformed Judaism, not a hybrid of law and grace, but a new creation. In the new creation, “neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.” The old categories — the categories by which the Judaizers were demanding conformity — have been abolished. What remains is the new creation in Christ, the Israel of God, the community of those who walk by the rule of the cross.

The letter ends as it began: with the gospel. Paul opened with grace and peace; he closes with “grace be with your spirit, brothers.” He opened with astonishment that they were deserting grace; he closes with the reminder that grace is still there, still sufficient, still the only ground on which any person, anywhere, stands before God. Galatians is, from first to last, a letter about grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes six chapters of doctrine and puts them to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life. A brother caught in any transgression is to be restored — the word for mending a net or setting a bone — in a spirit of gentleness, by people who keep watch on themselves (v. 1). Verse 2 calls this bearing one another’s burdens and so fulfilling the law of Christ, which Paul has already defined as love (5:14). Verses 3–5 explain why restoration goes wrong: self-deception (v. 3), a verdict reached by comparison (v. 4), and forgetting that each will carry his own load on the day of account (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as a Community of Restoration

The Reformed tradition has never regarded the church as merely a preaching station but as a communion of saints — a body committed to mutual care, discipline and restoration. Verse 1 is the practical expression of the justification theology of the whole letter. We deal gently with a failing brother because we know we stand only by grace; the man who forgets his own proneness to sin will always be a prosecutor, and the man who remembers it will be a restorer. Gentleness without truth produces sentimentality, and truth without gentleness produces further fracture. Both are failures of the same verse.

Verses 2 and 5 together give the balance that keeps a church healthy, and both errors are recognisable. What is crushing a man, others are commanded to help carry; what is properly his own — his obedience, his repentance, his answer at the last day — nobody can carry for him, and pretending otherwise is not kindness. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him and calls it strength, and the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church or his spouse and calls it fellowship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatian congregations were biting and devouring one another (5:15). Freedom had evidently been taken by some as licence, and the response of others was condemnation rather than restoration. Verse 1 corrects both errors at once, and v. 3 names what was fuelling the second: men who thought they were something. Verse 4 answers the comparison culture that ends chapter 5 in provoking and envying.

Now:Verse 2 puts a question that a warm and orthodox church can still fail: whose weight are you actually under — not whom you pray for, which costs very little, but whose burden has cost you a Saturday or money you had other plans for? And v. 4 is uncomfortably clarifying: when you last felt good about your Christian life, was that a judgement about your work or about somebody else’s?

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spiritual people restore a fallen brother gently, watching themselves lest they too be tempted.

Caught. Overtaken by a sin.

You who are spiritual. Led by the Spirit (5:25), not an élite.

Restore. Set a broken bone; mend a net. The aim is healing, not punishment.

Gentleness. The fruit of the Spirit in action.

What it does not mean. Gentle is not the same as soft: restoring names the sin and calls for repentance. But the goal is the person’s recovery, not the restorer’s satisfaction.

On a Tuesday. When a friend falls, go to them humbly, not to gossip but to help.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Carrying one another’s heavy loads fulfils the law of Christ, the law of love.

Burdens. Crushing weights: temptations, griefs, needs.

The law of Christ. His command to love (John 13:34). Not a new legalism.

What it does not mean. Not carrying what others refuse to carry themselves (v. 5; 2 Thessalonians 3:10), but helping those who are overloaded.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each person must examine his own work honestly before God, and each will carry his own load of responsibility.

Thinks he is something. Pride stops us bearing others’ burdens.

Test his own work. Compare yourself with God’s standard, not with others.

Burden and load. Verse 2 speaks of crushing weights to share; verse 5 of a soldier’s pack, personal responsibility no one else can carry. No contradiction.
verseByVerse.note: A “burden” in verse 2 is a crushing weight; a “load” in verse 5 is one’s own pack.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6 arrives without preliminaries and it is about money: let the one taught share all good things with the one who teaches. The verb is koinōneitō, from the word for fellowship, which tells you Paul did not regard the subject as a lower order of thing. Note also who is instructed — congregations to give, not teachers to raise support. The reversal has done real damage, because a man who must ask for his own living finds it very hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said one.

Verse 7 hardens the tone. God is not mocked uses a verb built on the word for the nose: nobody sneers at God and gets away with it. The farming principle that follows carries three certainties every agricultural town understood — you reap what you sowed, more than you sowed, and later than you sowed. It is the third that deceives people, because the gap is long enough to make the connection look unreal. Verse 8 names the two fields, and corruption is phthoran, decay: the flesh pays out not usually in catastrophe but in decomposition. The promise of eternal life to those who sow to the Spirit is not wages — six chapters forbid that — but the full growth of a life that was given.

Verse 9 assumes weariness rather than forbidding it, and Paul includes himself in the us. The one condition attached to the harvest is not achievement but persistence: if we do not give up. Verse 10 turns the weariness outward. As we have opportunity uses the same word as the season in v. 9, so the sowing season is now — which disposes of the commonest evasion, since it means while there is time, not when it is convenient. Doing good to everyone forbids the church turned inward; especially to the household of faith forbids a general benevolence that never reaches the believer two streets away.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest as the Motive of Present Faithfulness

Reformed ethics has always read present obedience in the light of a future harvest, and vv. 7–9 are where Paul states it most plainly. The believer does not do good in order to earn the harvest; the harvest is secured by grace, and this letter has spent six chapters proving that nothing a man sows can purchase eternal life. But the harvest is real and the reaping is certain, and the knowledge of it sustains present faithfulness. That is the farmer’s wisdom applied to the Christian life, not works-righteousness.

Verse 8 must be read in the terms already set, or it will contradict the letter. What it describes is a direction of life: the seed a man scatters shows which field he believes he lives in, and a person indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit for the same reason a living tree puts out leaves. And v. 6 grounds the support of gospel ministry in something older than church order — the Levites had no land and Israel ate with them, and Paul states the principle elsewhere as the labourer deserving his wages (1 Cor. 9:11; 1 Tim. 5:17–18), which is the Lord’s own saying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were weary — theologically confused, socially fragmented, and without Paul. The Judaizers’ programme was more structured and far more socially comfortable, and drifting toward it would have ended the trouble. Verse 9 is aimed exactly there: the harvest is coming, do not walk off the field. And v. 6 was not incidental either, since nothing in a congregation's life is a more exact readout of what its people actually believe than what happens to their money.

Now:Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable, which is why v. 8 so rarely frightens anyone into faithfulness; and v. 9 belongs to named people at the end of their strength, to whom Paul offers not encouragement about their prospects but a fact about the universe.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those taught the word should share material good things with those who teach them.

Share all good things. Support for pastors and teachers (1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).

On a Tuesday. Do you give to support those who teach you the word?

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God cannot be fooled: what we sow, we reap, to the flesh corruption, to the Spirit eternal life.

Not mocked. Literally, you cannot turn up your nose at God.

Sowing. Every choice is a seed. The harvest is certain, though delayed.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by works: sowing to the Spirit means living by the Spirit who has given us life.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers must not tire of doing good, for the harvest will come, especially towards the family of faith.

Weary. Doing good can be exhausting and seemingly fruitless.

In due season. God’s timing.

To everyone, especially. Love for all, with a first responsibility to fellow believers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The Cross and the New Creation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In v. 11 Paul takes the pen from his secretary and writes the closing paragraph himself, in large letters — the ancient equivalent of underlining hard enough to score the page. What he writes large is not doctrine but motive. Verse 12 says the men forcing circumcision want to make a good showing in the flesh and to avoid persecution for the cross, which had a concrete meaning in that century: Judaism was a recognised religion under Rome, and circumcised converts made the whole problem disappear for everyone. Verse 13 exposes the second motive, converts as trophies, and adds the detail that collapses the programme — the men selling the law do not keep it themselves, which 5:3 said it obligates them to.

Verse 14 answers with the sharpest contrast in the letter. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows, and far be it from me is his most violent negative. The cross was not yet jewellery: it was Rome’s method for killing slaves in public, and for a Pharisee it carried the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23 that Paul quoted at 3:13. The double crucifixion he describes runs both ways — the world's offers have lost their force on him, and he has lost his standing in its eyes, which is the harder half and precisely what the Judaizers were avoiding.

Verse 15 gives the verdict: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but a new creation — kainē ktisis, new in kind, the age to come arriving early in a person, not a renovation of the old. Verse 16 pronounces peace and mercy on all who walk by that rule, and on the Israel of God, the most argued-over phrase in the letter. Verse 17 closes the case not with an argument but with scars — stigmata, the brand of ownership — and v. 18 ends where 1:3 began, with grace, and with the word brothers standing last in the Greek sentence before the Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross as the Permanent Centre, and the Israel of God

Paul’s boast in v. 14 is the summary of everything the letter has argued. The cross is where the law’s curse was absorbed, where the old creation died and the new was born, and Reformed theology has always insisted it is not merely the entrance to the Christian life but its permanent centre — the ground the believer stands on at every moment from conversion to glory. This is Luther’s theology of the cross against a theology of glory: God’s ways are read from below, through shame and suffering, not from above through human notions of power and success.

On v. 16 everything turns on the small word kai, which can mean “and” or “even.” Read as “even the Israel of God,” the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together, are the Israel of God, which is the standard Reformed reading and is supported by 3:29 and 4:26. Read as simply “and,” a second group is in view, most naturally believing Jews. The first fits the letter’s whole argument best; the second is held by serious readers who love this book, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11. On what actually matters here nobody disagrees: whoever they are, the rule they walk by is the cross and the new creation, and no one enters that number by ancestry or by a mark.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted social safety, and vv. 12–13 name it without charity: circumcising the Gentiles satisfied the synagogue and left Rome uninterested. Verse 17 answers it with the marks Paul carried from his sufferings, among them the stoning at Lystra in Galatia itself (Acts 14:19).

Now:The test v. 13 puts to a softened conviction is not whether the reason is defensible but what the adjustment costs you. And v. 17 belongs to anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something unglamorous — Paul filed his scars under the same heading as the wounds of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes the final paragraph in his own large handwriting, exposing the motives of those who press circumcision.

Large letters. For emphasis, or because of poor eyesight (4:15).

A good showing in the flesh. They want to avoid persecution and to boast in the number of their converts.

Do not keep the law themselves. Hypocrisy.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then took the pen himself to finish; his large letters may reflect poor eyesight or simply emphasis.

verseByVerse.quote: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s only boast is the cross of Christ, through which the world is dead to him and he to the world.

Boast. Glory, take pride in.

The cross. A Roman instrument of shame, now his only pride.

Crucified to me. The world’s approval and values no longer have power over him.

For worship. “When I survey the wondrous cross… Forbid it, Lord, that I should boast, save in the death of Christ my God” (Isaac Watts).

verseByVerse.quote: For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What matters is not circumcision or its absence but new creation, and peace and mercy rest on all who follow this rule, the Israel of God.

A new creation. God’s new world begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The Israel of God. Where Christians differ. Some read this as believing Jews within the church, or Israel’s future salvation. Others, following the logic of the letter (3:7, 29), read it as the whole church of Jew and Gentile, the true Israel. Verdict: the whole church, God’s renewed Israel in Christ, without denying God’s purposes for Jewish people (Romans 11).
verseByVerse.note: Interpreters differ over whether “the Israel of God” means believing Jews or the whole church, Jew and Gentile together. The more persuasive reading is the whole church (compare 3:29).

verseByVerse.quote: From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul bears in his body the scars of his service to Jesus, the only marks that matter; and he ends with grace.

The marks of Jesus. Stigmata, brands like those on slaves or devotees. His scars from stoning and beatings (Acts 14:19; 2 Corinthians 11:23–25) are better proof of belonging than circumcision.

Grace. The letter that began with grace (1:3) ends with it.

For worship. Thank God for those who bear scars for Christ, and ask for courage to bear yours.
verseByVerse.note: The “marks” were the scars left by beatings and stoning — like the brands on a slave showing whom he belonged to.
